claims.text: The activity and selectivity of the PGM-based ethanol-oxidation catalyst are governed by the formation and removal of oxygen-bearing surface intermediates.
Multiple active metal sites with distinct electronic properties tune the coverage of reaction intermediates.
The tuning of intermediate coverage enables efficient 12-electron and 12-proton ethanol oxidation.
Changing electrode potential and electrolyte composition will alter adsorbate coverage and ethanol-oxidation pathways.
CO-like species and surface OH groups are important adsorbates on the catalyst's multiple active sites.
Synergy among diverse metal sites modifies the local electronic structure.
The modified electronic structure optimizes adsorption of key intermediates and promotes their oxidative removal.
Optimized adsorption and removal of intermediates promote complete ethanol oxidation through the 12-electron route.
The multi-element PGM catalyst will convert more ethanol to CO2 than a simpler Pt-based reference catalyst.
The multi-element PGM catalyst will exhibit more stable faradaic efficiency than the Pt-based reference.
The multi-element PGM catalyst will accumulate fewer partial ethanol-oxidation products than the Pt-based reference.
A single-metal Pt catalyst lacks synergy among chemically distinct metal sites.
The proposed effect applies at controlled electrode potentials and moderate temperatures relevant to direct ethanol fuel-cell anodes.
The proposed effect may fail for other fuels or under conditions that induce catalyst dissolution.
Previous studies reported strong catalytic performance for PGM-based nanoscale catalysts in ethanol oxidation.
Direct in-situ surface-spectroscopy evidence for the proposed ethanol-oxidation mechanism is lacking.
Absence of potential- or electrolyte-dependent changes in intermediate coverage and removal would falsify the proposed coverage-mediated mechanism.
Failure to outperform a simpler Pt catalyst would falsify the proposed synergistic multi-metal-site explanation.
